findings.evidence: "Riders may request a fare adjustment through the mobile app. Station staff can also help with the same request in person."
findings.fix: Replace with content actually describing the accessibility improvement (e.g., the platform/parking work shown in the image below), or move this paragraph to a section about fares.
findings.violation: This paragraph is about fare adjustments, not accessibility, so the content doesn't match the "Accessibility improvements" heading it sits under.

findings.evidence: "Passengers can check real time arrivals by calling rider services. Updates post to the schedule page within one business day."
findings.fix: Remove or relocate this paragraph to a relevant section (e.g., real-time arrivals or contact info), and replace with accessibility-specific content.
findings.violation: This is generic real-time-arrival/phone-service information unrelated to accessibility, reinforcing that the section's body text doesn't match its own heading.

findings.evidence: "Passengers may request a fare adjustment through the mobile app. Station staff can also help with the same request in person." (identical to #s1-p1)
findings.fix: Write weekend-service-specific copy (e.g., about weekend schedules/frequency) and remove the duplicated fare-adjustment boilerplate.
findings.violation: This text is a verbatim duplicate of the paragraph in the "Accessibility improvements" section and has nothing to do with weekend service.

findings.fix: Add a `<caption>` (e.g., "Weekend zone status") and wrap the header row in `<thead>` and data rows in `<tbody>`.
findings.violation: The table has no `<caption>` and no `<thead>`/`<tbody>` structure, so screen reader users aren't told what the table represents.

findings.evidence: "Local residents should review the updated schedule through the mobile app. Station staff can also help with the same request in person."
findings.fix: Rewrite the second sentence to match the actual action, e.g., "Station staff can also help you review the schedule in person."
findings.violation: "the same request" has no antecedent - the first sentence describes reviewing a schedule, not making a request, so the second sentence doesn't logically follow (leftover boilerplate from the fare-adjustment paragraph reused elsewhere).

findings.evidence: "Passengers should review the updated schedule through the mobile app. The change takes effect on the following service day."

findings.evidence: "Local residents can check real time arrivals by calling rider services. Updates post to the schedule page within one business day."
findings.fix: Keep this content in one place (likely a "Real-time arrivals" or contact section) and remove the duplicate from #s1-p2.

findings.fix: Use a real `<button>` element with a descriptive accessible name (e.g., `aria-label="Delete"`) instead of a styled div/image.
findings.violation:
This appears to be an interactive delete control but is a non-interactive `
`/`` with no `role="button"`, no `tabindex`, no keyboard handler, and an empty `alt`, making it invisible and unusable to screen reader and keyboard users.

findings.evidence:
`
Confirm your order
` appears before `
...` and `
...` in the markup
findings.fix: Reorder the elements in the DOM to match the intended reading order (Choose a plan → Enter payment details → Confirm your order) and use a semantic `<ol>` for the steps instead of `<div>`s, removing reliance on CSS `order`.
findings.violation: The visual order is controlled by CSS `order` (1,2,3 → "Choose a plan", "Enter payment details", "Confirm your order"), but the DOM/source order is reversed (3,2,1); screen readers and keyboard tab order follow DOM order, so assistive-technology users will encounter the steps in the wrong sequence.

findings.evidence: `For the full list of upcoming adjustments, read the accessibility improvements list.`
findings.fix: Make the link text, surrounding text, and href all describe the same destination, e.g., link text "view the schedule changes list" pointing to a schedule-changes URL.
findings.violation: The link text ("accessibility improvements list") doesn't match the surrounding sentence (about "upcoming adjustments"/schedule changes) or the href target (`/fares/history`), creating three mutually inconsistent signals about where the link goes.

findings.fix: Add a visible text cue (e.g., "(required)") and/or `aria-required="true"` on the input, not just a color change on the label.
findings.violation: The label is styled red with no accompanying text, icon, or ARIA attribute explaining why - relying on color alone to convey status (e.g., required/error) fails users who can't perceive color (WCAG 1.4.1).

findings.fix: Only set `aria-invalid="true"` after actual validation fails, add `aria-describedby="s3-form-promo-error"` on the input, and replace "Error." with a specific message (e.g., "Promo code not recognized").
findings.location: Section "Schedule changes", form promo code field (#s3-form-promo-label, #promo, #s3-form-promo-error)
findings.violation: `aria-invalid="true"` is hard-coded in the initial markup (so the field is announced as invalid before any user interaction or submission), and the error message span is not linked to the input via `aria-describedby`, so screen reader users won't hear "Error." when focused on the field; the message is also non-descriptive.
